Helldivers 2 gameplay mostly consists of you and your squad deploying to different planets to complete operations that have the purpose of winning the galactic war and protecting Super Earth.

 You can play alone but its even better if you play with friends or with strangers in voice chat, in particular in higher difficulty missions where things get chaotic, which usually leads to insane moments where you somehow make it out alive out of a situation that looked impossible to survive. In higher difficulties it is almost impossible to complete operations by yourself, often needing teammates that are able to coordinate with you to complete the objectives. 

 The game also features a few currencies, some to upgrade your destroyers capability, others to buy stratagems, outfits and other items.

 The different factions, different creatures such as bile titans and hulks, and planets provide variety in terms of gameplay, difficulty or visuals , some planets are stunning visually, some creatures are immune to certain weapons, different objectives require different strategies. Another factor that helps in gameplay variety is the huge collection of stratagems, where you have support weapons, orbital or eagle strikes and turrets or sentries, this also provides different possibilities when facing a certain mission.

The only problem is that after several missions, even though there are different factions planets and operations, it might get repetitive, and it gets worse if you play to farm items such as samples, which is not bad, but it usually leads to very repetitive gameplay, so ideally don't stress about quickly getting everything max level and getting game items and focus more on enjoying the gameplay. 

 When it comes to performance, my specs are not very strong but i am able to play the game at medium settings with around 60fps, which is acceptable for me, if you have better specs then you are probably fine, if your system is weaker then you should be a bit more careful with graphic settings.

 Obviously this game is great, especially because i cannot talk bad about it, since it would be considered treason, and I get the honor of dying for SUPER EARTH, it has potential to create a lot of epic moments and i highly recommend you play this with friends and try out the different stratagems.

I had written a good long draft of this review once, I think it's really important to share my experience with this game, but I wrote a comment this morning and realised it's much shorter (and better) at explaining what I have to say, so here it is:

"For me I would have just liked to feel like the studio weren't conceited lying douchebags sneaking in changes and reducing progression to only paid DLC, and the community were seemingly anything but a steaming pile of teamkilling, gaslighting and death threat-making turds. There were so many nice, friendly, helpful and cooperative people as well, and it would be really so much fun with those people, but I've never seen so many griefers or people refusing to cooperate in a CO-OP GAME it blew my mind a bit, and just wondering when TK'ing might suddenly happen and how many more people I would have to block wore me down before I could bring myself to find a way to make it work (like look for a regular group to play with and make a separate discord, which I was in the middle of doing). The game definitely has issues but apart from being lucky with not experiencing many bugs if at all on my setup, the gameplay loop was so much fun and I really could have been playing HD2 non-stop if TK'ing and griefing/crybaby glazing wasn't so common in-game through the first year. I played almost every day from March '24 to Jan '25 then stopped for that reason. Started again for Cyberstan, then quit as soon as the doxxing happened and I saw all the reactions, including AH's limp denialism of any serious problem with their community, or their culpability in making it what it is.
But their pattern of not taking feedback seriously was becoming quite obvious too, with these tonedeaf posts and a gradual reversion of much of what made the 60-Day Patch work as both a game fix and an olive branch with the fans

If I wasn't driven away by all this, I'd have given up on grinding Diff 1's and just been buying Super Credits to keep up with warbonds by now, and I wouldn't have minded the price really, there's some fun stuff they add and the grind could always be a backup plan if a WB didn't seem worth ten bucks. That's easily 14 warbond's worth of money they missed out on in my case and there was more to be released and bought. Now they can imagine how many times over that may be true, for thousands of other players who cared enough to say something together and would have supported the studio if their money, time and intelligence were respected, but now have just had enough."

TL:DR: Numerous problems with stability and performance, arguments over balance and the studio being pig-headed or just bad at PR are big issues for people - A major problem is progression had almost completely stalled, new players might have plenty to unlock but be warned that for a year DLC has been the only way to get gear and recent changes may not stick, so maybe check back in a few months. If you get high on drama, love to argue in chat or upset people for fun then this is the game (or rather forums) for you, but if you can't tolerate this even slightly and want to know this game is being handled competently, I would avoid.

This review was written with AI because, much like the developers, I no longer have any interest in investing more time into this IP.

Having played intermittently since about a month after launch, I can say HD2 is at once one of the most fun and most disappointing titles of my gaming career. 
At its best, this game yields some of the most cinematic and fun moments you can have in an online shooter with your friends. Having your back pressed against the wall by legions of undemocratic scum with the success of your mission on the line, then being able to cut a swath through your enemies with some incredible airstrike or mech or other weaponry to get to your extraction point can be exhilarating and cathartic in a way that I don't have the language to express properly. I've lost track of how many incredible war stories I've generated in the battle for managed democracy. Save for the occasional technical hiccup off of limited-time events, the game has been very reliable for me technically as well.
My main gripe is with the development, as I feel that Arrowhead is (though leagues better than some competitors) ultimately not running the game's live-service elements well. For a long time there was a consensus that they were basically heroes, paying constant and close attention to the pulse of the game. Issues like requiring a PSN were the fault of mean old Sony, and Arrowhead were the plucky indie team continuously addressing player concerns and throwing out new content like candy. With time, though, I've come to realize there are a few core issues that really handicap the game's success.
The first is not having a proper balance team or strategy. Time and again, this has lead to the team throwing out balance changes in very awkward ways: if a stratagem or gun becomes the meta, it gets nerfed; if a weapon is too weak, it gets either barely improved or entirely neglected; older items (like the base Liberator) aren't re-evaluated to keep up with the current threats of the war and basically become obsolete. In addition, the developers only playtest a limited selection of difficulties, meaning that some of the higher tiers are unreasonable for anyone but those with the highest understanding of the game's systems and how to abuse them. Balancing should be an overhead consideration, not a series of band-aids applied when someone complains too loudly one way or the other-- in that respect listening to the community is sometimes a bad idea.
Second is hidden changes to balance that aren't listed in patch notes. Armor ratings, for instance, were only shown in vague terms on weapons & stratagems early on. With time, dataminers and eventually Arrowhead themselves have acknowledged other subtiers and values which make the durabilities of enemies and players far more involved than simple light/medium/heavy penetration. Changes have historically been made to these and other values without any indication to the community; one of the most recent instances was a claimed durability buff to mechs, but an unmentioned increase on penetration for automatons that ultimately negated that buff. I understand that the average player doesn't need to know the exact nuance of every single statistical value in the game, but I do believe that altering characteristics of the enemies and equipment without indicating them is bogus.
Last is what I see as a growing disconnect from the community at large. Arrowhead's most recent Steam news post is evidence of this, the most disheartening issue of all. It was apparently worth an entire solitary announcement post to declare they were capping Super Credit earnings, and to frame it as a blessing to a begging community from on high as if it was some sort of profound repair to the game's economy rather than just kneecapping a nearly-irrelevant issue. Why should I care if someone piles up some currency when the only thing that means is that they might be able to bring some different weapons into the fight alongside me? I understand that protecting paid currency is a natural thing for developers to do, but the framing of its presentation (in conjunction with other existing issues) makes me feel like a gap's opened between the developers and the average joe player. It feels especially disingenuous for this to receive top billing while stratagem bouncing and countless other issues have lingered for, in some cases, years-- there's a trail of broken and half delivered promises that make it difficult to take the team at their word, let alone watch them praise themselves for solving a non-issue on players' parts.
TLDR: Ultimately Arrowhead's attempts to maintain the game as a service have degraded into a muddle of kneejerk/secretive balance changes, and a disconnect from the wider community. It's fundamentally a great game and there have been nice changes recently (quite like the new campaign mechanic and it's great to see new weapons available outside of warbonds), but ultimately the developers' repeated failure to sustain transparency and consistency means I have to recommend against buying it as-is.

Whenever you see Helldivers 2 and wonder, "Why does this game have so many negative reviews?", this is one of the reasons.

The core gameplay is fantastic. Few games capture the chaos of fighting overwhelming hordes of bugs, robots, and aliens as well as Helldivers 2. The problem is that many of the game's biggest frustrations have existed for months, and in some cases years, without meaningful fixes.

The developers often defend certain mechanics as "realistic" or "chaotic," but too often that feels like an excuse for poor game design. Almost everything you bring into a mission can kill you. Orbital strikes kill you. Air support kills you. Turrets kill you. Mines kill you. Flamethrowers burn you. Gas weapons poison you. Drones can shoot you. Setting up defensive positions often feels like you're creating hazards for your own team rather than tools to fight the enemy.

Friendly fire can be funny. Chaos can be fun. But when nearly every piece of equipment becomes a liability, it stops feeling like a deliberate design choice and starts feeling frustrating. That's not realism—it's bad gameplay.

Then there are the crashes, persistent bugs, and balance issues. On higher difficulties, the game increasingly pushes players toward a handful of optimal loadouts. Instead of encouraging experimentation, many weapons and stratagems feel like traps compared to the few meta choices that consistently work.

The biggest issue for me is that the game often discourages the very thing it's best at: fighting enemies. At the highest difficulties, enemy spawns can become so relentless that the optimal strategy is frequently to avoid combat, sprint between objectives, and complete tasks as quickly as possible. The game shines when you're standing your ground against impossible odds, not when you're running circles around the map turning valves, aligning radio signals, or tossing grenades into holes while avoiding endless waves of enemies.

Helldivers 2 is still fun. That's what makes all of this so frustrating. The foundation is excellent, but it feels like the developers keep adding new content while long-standing problems remain unresolved—and sometimes new updates introduce even more issues.

I have over 900 hours in Helldivers 2, and for most of that time I genuinely loved this game. The core gameplay is some of the best fun I've had in years. If this review were based solely on gameplay, it would be an easy recommendation.

Unfortunately, the developer, Arrowhead, has steadily eroded that goodwill.

The biggest problem isn't a single balance patch or one bad update. It's the pattern. Time and again, the community raises major concerns, only for them to be ignored until player numbers drop or backlash becomes impossible to avoid. At that point, Arrowhead promises they'll "do better," acknowledges player feedback, and outlines a new direction. Then months pass with little meaningful follow-through before the cycle repeats.

Meanwhile, bugs that have existed for years remain unresolved. At some point it's difficult to tell whether they're considered bugs anymore or simply permanent features of the game. Instead of focusing on improving and stabilizing the core experience, the emphasis often feels like it's on shipping the next Warbond.

That approach has slowly killed my enthusiasm. I kept taking breaks, hoping the game would eventually receive the improvements that had been promised. Instead, every time I came back I was further behind on Warbonds, faced an even larger grind to catch up, and had a harder time finding open missions. Rather than making me excited to return, the game increasingly felt like it was punishing me for not treating it like a second job.

What finally convinced me to leave this review was Arrowhead's recent messaging around the game's future. After repeatedly talking about finally focusing on the game's almost nonexistent endgame, one of their next major announcements was that they intended to dedicate development effort toward combating cheaters. In over 900 hours, I can remember encountering maybe two obvious cheaters. This simply isn't one of the community's biggest problems.

Even more frustrating was that there wasn't even a timeline for this work. It wasn't presented as a completed improvement or something already in testing—it was simply announced as a priority while many long-standing gameplay issues remain unresolved. Considering that the most common cheating revolves around Super Credits, it's difficult not to feel that protecting premium currency is receiving more attention than the issues players have been asking about for months.

Maybe that's not Arrowhead's intent, but it's certainly the impression their priorities create.

Helldivers 2 is still an incredibly fun game at its core. That's what makes this so disappointing. The potential is still there, and that's why I've waited so long hoping things would improve. Instead, I've watched promises repeatedly fail to materialize while the game becomes increasingly difficult for returning or new players to keep up with. It's a shame really, the game deserves a far better company behind it.

For new players, I'd recommend looking elsewhere unless you're prepared for a significant time commitment or spending a substantial amount of money to catch up on years of Warbonds. If Arrowhead ever follows through on the improvements they've been promising for so long, I'd be happy to change this review. Until then, I can't recommend it despite how much fun the game itself can be.

I don't think I've ever seen a game before that was successful in spite of the devs and not because of them at this level. The core game itself is still fun and that's just solo diving, and obviously one of the most well known aspects of this game is how absurdly chaotic it can get with others. I will say too that as someone rocking AMD and running Linux (Mint btw), the game is pretty stable overall, so FWIW I'd take actual hardware into consideration as from what I've seen its largely Nvidia and/or Intel users that are really getting hit with that stuff far as I can tell. 

The real issues lie with Arrowhead themselves. They quote their own philosophy as "a game for everyone is a game for no one", which is all fine and great until you get to a point where your by far most popular title is constantly flip flopping back and forth on what its supposed to be. They seem to really want to have this seriously strategic tactical shooter idea in mind, which is fine, but for years the entire game has been marketed as the total opposite. Helldivers are simultaneously supposed to fulfill a grunt fantasy yet are also walking one man armies raining destruction down with stratagems and their super destroyer. Some seem to want something gritty and slower paced and tactical while also having stratagems like a flag of Super Earth to wave around and hit things or a backpack mounted hellbomb you can use to be the bomb. Grunts don't get their own special spaceship and last I checked SEAF wasn't running around with heavy energy weapons and super munitions being dropped on demand whenever they want while also decked out in shiny buff boosting armor and billowing capes. Expendable as they may still be if a grunt fantasy was really the core objective there'd be an ODST style thing going on with the SEAF. Just look at the entire ambiance of the game itself where a voteless brain scan shows them lighting up at the sight of a forklift or literally anything the democracy officer on your destroyer says and tell me with a straight face this was ever some super serious thing, even with events like Malevelon Creek. 

Point being AH got lightning in a bottle and doesn't exactly seem to know what to really do with it, and thats not even discussing the whole issue with the warbond system as it stands now, or the constant struggle of having to find out what really got changed because for whatever reason they can't actually be bothered to list them in the changelogs, the overall rugpull that was Cyberstan, etc. 

Summing all this yapping up, the issue is basically whether or not Arrowhead is going to go full Gaijin, only at least WT had the decency to ultimately not get paywalled behind 40 bucks. There was a point in time where HD2 was *the* game, something highly impressive given its only been out for two years, and Arrowhead doesn't really seem to care much anymore to bring that kind of magic back. And if they do then they have a long way to go in actually communicating that.

In my very first mission a Level 120+ joined me, and as I was still learning the controls and how the game works I accidentally blew him up. After he came back with reinforcement, he nuked me, then danced on my corpse and quit. I thought to myself, "oh boy, this game might not work out..." However, luckily this does not represent the community, in fact it was the rare exception. Since then I met with a lot of different players and playstyles, most of them are not just very understanding but particularly willing to help. Occasionally some people will join you even without sending an SOS Beacon. Some people will teach you and explain the basics and the little extras that you need to know. Overall its a fun community. 

As for the game itself, oh boy I like the humour, however after introductions you rarely encounter it. The missions vary quite a bit, throughout several systems, planets and difficulty. There is a system for each type of player for PvE. The beginning might be a bit of a slag, but after you unlock more stuff - ship upgrades, weapons, difficulties and missions, it branches out nicely. 

Stratagems vary from niche to situational use to useful to broad, so you can have many options for playstyle and weapons to suit your own taste. Firearms are good, its nice and impactful shooting stuff. Blowing up stuff is even more fun the more you use it. And dont get me started on turrets, vehicles, robots and backpacks.

The game is certainly not for everyone, and some missions and some grinding can take more time than you would like. But overall, its a good experience and can recommend it.

This game is definitely more high-octane than most. Lots of enemies and lots of shooting—what more could you ask for? The visuals are nice and the game runs well. The controls are easy to learn, and the overall gameplay loop feels pretty polished. Procedural generation also goes a long way for immersion, making every planet feel different from the last. There are several planets to choose from at any given moment, and a variety of missions for certain factions within those planets. Plus, there's like 100 different guns and dozens of stratagems & upgrades to help you spread democracy more effectively. If you enjoy conquering hostile worlds every second of every day, look no further, soldier.

If you enjoy shooters, Helldivers 2 is definitely worth checking out. It's a fast-paced, objective-based extraction shooter where you complete missions, call in powerful ordnance from your destroyer or Eagle air support, and fight your way through hordes of enemies. The sound design is phenomenal, the sci-fi/space atmosphere is well through out, and the huge variety of ordinances keeps every mission feeling fresh and chaoticly fun. Easily one of the best shooters I've played in a long time.
